title: 1960 AHSME Problem 33
statement: You are given a sequence of \(58\) terms; each term has the form \(P+n\) where \(P\) stands for the product \(2\cdot3\cdot5\cdots61\) of all prime numbers less than or equal to \(61,\) and \(n\) takes, successively, the values \(2,\) \(3,\) \(4,\) \(\ldots,\) \(59.\) Let \(N\) be the number of primes appearing in this sequence. Then \(N\) is:

solutions.text:
For each \(n\) in the given range, choose a prime divisor \(p\) of \(n.\) Since \(p\le59,\) it is one of the factors of \(P.\) Therefore \(p\) divides \(P+n.\) Moreover \(P+n>p,\) so \(P+n\) is composite. No term is prime, and \(N=0.\)

Thus, the correct answer is A.
hints: Every \(n\) from \(2\) through \(59\) has a prime divisor at most \(59\)
That same prime divisor divides both \(P\) and \(n\)
